g.title: n0
g.text: and tunes to a standard broadcast frequency

g.title: narrative
g.text: Person‑X powered on an analogue radio
and tuned to what appeared to be a standard broadcast frequency.
The presenter’s voice was immediately distinctive: sharp, forceful,
and issuing instructions in a tone reminiscent of military command.
Seeking to move away from the transmission,
Person‑X adjusted the dial to a different frequency.
Upon reaching the new position on the dial,
the expected station or static emerged clearly and
without distortion for approximately half a second or longer.
After this brief interval of normal reception, the audio abruptly shifted,
and the same presenter’s voice reappeared
— as though the transmission had overridden the new frequency.
Further attempts to tune away produced the same result.
Multiple points on the dial, which should have contained unrelated stations
or background static, instead resolved back into the same commanding voice.
The overall effect was that of a single broadcast dominating the band.
From a technical standpoint, Person‑X acknowledges
that a strong, nearby RF source could saturate the radio’s front end,
causing the receiver to momentarily lock
onto the correct frequency before collapsing
into a single dominant signal across the dial.
This mechanism is feasible at a very local level.
